common_name: Juneprince Peach (USDA-ARS Byron Georgia Early-Season Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Juneprince carries the moderate-to-high chill requirement typical of the Byron, Georgia program, so it performs best in zones 6-9 rather than the mildest Gulf Coast sites.

directions: Juneprince is an early-ripening, self-fruitful yellow freestone peach from the USDA-ARS stone fruit breeding program at Byron, Georgia, part of the same naming lineage that later produced Julyprince, Augustprince, and Rubyprince. As its name suggests, it ripens earlier in the season than most of its later-named siblings, giving Southeastern growers an early-summer harvest ahead of the main midsummer peach crop. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, thin fruit early to improve size, and prune annually to an open-center form for good light penetration and airflow in humid summers.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Byron, GA Fruit and Tree Nut Research

common_name: Augustprince Peach (USDA-ARS Byron Georgia Late-Season Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Augustprince ripens later than most of its '-prince' siblings and, like them, needs a moderate-to-high winter chill best met in zones 6-9.

directions: Augustprince is a late-season yellow freestone peach from the USDA-ARS stone fruit breeding program at Byron, Georgia, part of the same '-prince' naming lineage as Juneprince, Julyprince, and Rubyprince. Ripening in August, it extends the Byron program's harvest window well past the midsummer peaches that make up most of the lineage, giving Southeastern home orchardists fresh peaches later in the season. Plant in full sun with good drainage, thin fruit early for size, and prune annually to an open-vase form for airflow and disease management in the humid Southeast.

common_name: Mother Vine Scuppernong (Historic Roanoke Island Heritage Muscadine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring on a strong overhead arbor or high-wire trellis; this heritage selection shares the vigor and disease resistance of ordinary Scuppernong but is propagated specifically from the historic Roanoke Island vine.

directions: The Mother Vine is a specific, individual scuppernong-type muscadine grapevine on Roanoke Island, North Carolina, believed to be more than 400 years old and still bearing fruit, making it one of the oldest cultivated grapevines in North America and the ancestral plant behind the entire muscadine grape industry. A handful of specialty nurseries propagate and sell rooted cuttings taken directly from this historic vine as a named heritage selection distinct from ordinary nursery-grown Scuppernong stock, valued as much for its history as for its bronze-green, musky-sweet fruit. Culture matches standard Scuppernong: plant on a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis in full sun and well-drained soil, where the extremely vigorous, long-lived vine needs little beyond annual winter pruning back to short spurs. Like other muscadines it shows strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease and other problems that limit European wine grapes in the humid South.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension — Muscadine Grapes
